# Abstract {.unnumbered}

OpenPFC is a framework for solving partial differential equations on
structured, periodic, MPI-distributed grids, with matching CPU and GPU
execution paths. Its original target was the phase-field crystal (PFC) model,
but the architecture — a domain decomposition, a distributed field, a
pluggable spectral or finite-difference stack, and a session that wires them
from JSON — is not specific to PFC.

This report describes the fourteen applications shipped with OpenPFC 0.2.
They span fourth- through tenth-order spatial operators, conserved and
non-conserved dynamics, dispersive and dissipative behaviour, single-field and
coupled multi-field systems, and both spectral and finite-difference
discretisations.

Three claims run through the report.

The first is that **high differential order is not high implementation
complexity in a spectral code**. A sixth-order elastohydrodynamic operator and
a fourth-order Cahn–Hilliard operator differ, in the source, by the polynomial
returned from one function. The equivalent real-space stencils would not be
comparable in effort. What high order does cost is stiffness, and the report
is explicit about how exponential time differencing absorbs it.

The second is that **the same application source runs on a laptop core and on
sixteen nodes of a GPU supercomputer**. Chapter @sec-scalability reports
measured curves on LUMI-G out to 128 GCDs across 16 nodes: strong scaling at
82% efficiency over a fourfold increase in ranks, and weak scaling at constant
work per GCD ending on 8.59 billion cells. The application sources are
unchanged between the one-GCD and the 128-GCD runs. The chapter also compares
the spectral and finite-difference paths on the same equation, and is explicit
about the one axis of that comparison the measurements do not settle.

The third is that **the two discretisations compose**. @sec-alloy-dendrite is
a thermo-solutal-elastic dendritic solidification model: a quantitative
dilute-alloy phase field with anti-trapping current, coupled to solute, to
temperature through latent heat, and to quasi-static elasticity through a
composition- and temperature-dependent eigenstrain whose energy feeds back
into the phase-field driving force. The local physics runs on high-order
finite differences with a halo exchange; elliptic mechanical equilibrium is
elsewhere in the same time step, solved spectrally on the same
decomposition. At the calibrated coupling the elastic energy of the solutal
misfit slows the dendrite tip by 17 % and fattens it by 11 %, while the
selection parameter moves 2.5 % — the elasticity slides the operating point
along the solvability curve rather than changing the selection. With the
temperature field on, the solutal and thermal eigenstrains oppose each other
and together store a third of what the solutal misfit stores alone.

None of the three claims is asserted without a number behind it. Where a
property has not been measured, the report says so — and where a number
depends on a parameter of the *method* rather than of the physics, as the
dendrite's magnitude does on the liquid-shear regularisation, the report
gives the range rather than the digit.
